Africa: Okavango, upper Zambezi and Kasai River system. Type locality: Okavango River.

Parauchenoglanis ngamensis is currently distributed across the Okavango and the upper Zambezi, Kwanza, and Kasai (sub)basins of southern Africa.
Favours rocky habitats or marginal vegetation in slow-flowing rivers and lagoons, often taking shelter under trees.
Grows quite large. Best suited to the larger aquarium.

In its natural habitat its diet consists of small fishes and invertebrates like snails, shrimps and insects. In the aquarium it will eat a variety of foods: tablet and pellet foods with a good quality flake and frozen bloodworms. Also relishes live worms such as the common garden worm, making sure that there has been no weedkiller on the premises, and white worm.

Not a predator as such, so should be safe to house with smaller species. Peaceful large catfish which will do well in company of larger characins from Africa and large barbs. 'Grunts' when taken out of the water.
Eggs are large and relatively few, suggesting parental care, but no details are known.

This genus, which includes another 8 species, is quite difficult to identify, and juveniles can have different markings and colouration to the adults. First transferred into Parauchenoglanis by Skelton in 1993.

Etymology: Parauchenoglanis: para-, near, referring to similarity and/or close relationship with Auchenoglanis. ngamensis: -ensis, suffix denoting place: Lake Ngami district, Botswana, type locality.

A 2024 paper in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society by Yonela Sithole et al. used molecular and morphological data to explore hidden species diversity within this species. They redescribe P. patersoni, confined to the Okavango and upper Zambezi (sub)basins, and describe eight new species: two from the Kwanza Basin and six from the Kasai sub-basin, P. ernstswartzi, P. dolichorhinus, P. poikilos, P. megalasma, P. lueleensis, P. luendaensis and P. chiumbeensis.

IUCN Red List: Least Concern. The species has a wide distribution with no known major widespread threats, although diamond mining is an important threat in small rivers in the Kasai region.
